utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Hedaraly, is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Prosecution would like to call Witness 52 in Zagreb through videolink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let us see whether the videolink with Zagreb is functioning well. Yes. I can see you in Zagreb. The -- I see, apparently, the witness and the representative of the registry. Could you inform the Chamber who else is in the room in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. On behalf of the registry from the field office in Zagreb, I can confirm that all the technical equipment is set. Over here in the courtroom -- in the field office with us is technician, for now, until we start with the testimony and when we start he will leave the room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I ask you, Mrs. Urukalo, whether you can hear me in a language you understand? If you look at your screen, you will see who is talking to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I stand up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you see me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look at that man.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, I see a man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I am the Judge, together with two other Judges in this case. You can see me, I'm wearing the red robe, together with the other Judges. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you will not hear my own voice because I do not speak your language, so, therefore, what I say is translated to you so you may hear the voice of someone else, but he or she translates to you what I say. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not hear anybody else but this lady now, you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This lady is translating in your language what I say. Now, similarly, what you tell us is translated to us as well, so even though we do not speak the same language, through the assistance of the interpreters, we can understand what you're telling us, and you can understand what we are saying. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, it is clear. What you have just now told me is clear to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, can you see us on the screen. We see you on our screens through the camera which is in that room. We can see you; you can see us. Is that clear to you as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, so now you are -- although you are in Zagreb, you are in a courtroom because we can see you in this courtroom, and you give your testimony in this courtroom, which is a public session. Is that clear to you as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Later, questions will be put to you, not by me, but I'll tell who is putting the questions to you and then you're invited to answer these questions. But before you do so, the Rules which are applicable in this courtroom, require that you make a solemn declaration, that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Now, I do understand that you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have said it once, and I can't say it 100 times. I already said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Let me just -- we have to go through it step by step. Since you cannot read, I will -- I will give the words that we expect you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Therefore, I will tell you what this solemn declaration, what words we expect you to speak. Could you please repeat my words and I do it bit by bit. Could you please repeat my words. I solemnly declare ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch this word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat -- could you repeat the words as I speak them. I'll speak them slowly, and I invite you to repeat those words. These words are: I solemnly declare ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Woe is me. I solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next words are, that I will speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That I will speak the truth and I have told the truth. Woe is me, why should I have to go through all this again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, could you repeat also the following words: The whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've said what I had to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And there you are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And -- yes. What you will tell this afternoon when you're responding to questions, you're also going to tell us the whole truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, on behalf of the Defence we accept that as a legitimate declaration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then -- now, if you would look to your screen, then you will see Mr. Hedaraly. Mr. Hedaraly will ask you some questions. Mr. Hedaraly is from the Prosecutor's office. Carefully listen to him and try to answer as good as you can the questions he puts to you. You'll see him. He has not a red robe; he has a black robe. Yes. Mr. Hedaraly, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. Urukalo.

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Just before we start, can you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: You have my first and last names.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I know I do. I'm just asking to confirm that for the Court.

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: It's Draginja Urukalo. What else?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please confirm that your date of birth is 15 December 1922?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we can 65 ter 5495 on the screen, and that is tab 1 for Mr. Registrar in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Urukalo, the -- the court officer in Zagreb is showing you a document. Can you look at the bottom right of that document and tell us if you are the one that has placed that X there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And did you -- and yesterday did you have a chance to review this statement, and by that I mean, was it read back to you in your own language?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: It was read to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And when it was read to you, did it accurately reflect what you told the members of the Office of the Prosecutor with whom you met in 2003?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: It did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And that which was read back to you, was it the truth?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: It was the truth. I said what I said, and I said what I had remembered.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if you were asked questions similar to the ones you were asked then, the answers of which are in your statements, would you give the same answers in court today?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: Why wouldn't I? I said what I said, and that's the long and the short of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this time I would like 65 ter 5495 to be admitted into evidence pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number P964.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P964 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mrs. Urukalo, I have a few questions for you and this is mainly to clarify some of the points that are already in your statement that you reviewed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: My first question, in your statement at paragraph 3, there's a reference to people leaving the village on a Friday evening. And my question for you is the following.

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did anyone tell you why they were leaving?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: Nobody told me anything. I didn't know, but I could only see that the people were fleeing in vehicles, in tractors, leaving their houses. Everything went down the drain, the grain, the things that -- livestock and nobody knew who was doing it, or why.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And in the next paragraph, you discuss Croatian soldiers entering your village. Now, was that on the same day, on the Friday, or was that on the next day, on the Saturday?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: It was not immediately on Friday. It was afterwards, when all these troops flocked in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Do you know if that was the following day or was it several days after the first day when people left?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: It was later that these people came, in a day or two. When these people left on Friday, immediately on Saturday, these other people flooded the place, the troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And when they came in, in your statement you said they were shooting all around. Did they say anything to you or did you say anything to them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: They were shooting. What could they say to us? They were going through the village and shooting, and people were just looking where to hide, and where could one hide? They were just shooting. And they barged in the houses as well. Though I have to take this off, I can't stand these. Can I be without these?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is somehow uncomfortable.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Maybe we can adjust the volume. I don't know if that's the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: In your statement, in paragraph 4, you refer to some of the soldiers calling you a Chetnik mother. And I understand that you want to make a correction to that today?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: No. They did not say Chetnik mother to me. What they said to me was Chetnik whore and that's what I said and that's what they said to me. No, you are just twisting things around. It was not Chetnik mother that they called me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to move to what the soldiers actually did, and I know this could be difficult, so if any time you need a break or a moment just feel free to ask the Judges, because I want to make sure we get the sequence of events correctly. Now, in your statement, you refer to some soldiers that made you strip. And my question is were these the same soldiers than the ones who called you a Chetnik whore?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: How should I know? I wasn't in my right mind. Some people were coming, others were going. How could I know? Who would know?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: How many Croatian soldiers entered the village on that day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: Who have counted them, for heaven's sake. Who could have counted them. Some were coming in, others were leaving. How should I know how many of them they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Was it a large group, was it more than ten, was it just one or few?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: Woe is me. Who could have counted them? I have no idea how many of them there were. I was so concerned for my own safety, and it wasn't easy, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me go to that neighbour of yours, Dusan Urukalo. Do you know how old he was at that time? Was he older than you or younger than you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: He was older than me. The poor guy has died and his wife has died.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 5497 on the screen. And Mr. Registrar in Zagreb, that is a series of two photographs that are at tab 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Urukalo, can you see these photographs that are in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Does that accurately represent your -- the backyard behind your house?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: Yes. Outside the house, looking from the street, in front of the door, this basketball post, and they had me strip and they had me play. Only my knickers, my underwear remained on me and he, the wretched chap, had to strip naked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. President, can I have 65 ter 5496 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number P965.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P965 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Urukalo, I now want to move to just a little bit later when your grandson arrived at your village. When he arrived, were the other soldiers still there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: They left through the village in the direction of our cooperative, to Dzelanil [phoen], Marici, I'm not sure. But I didn't even recognise him. In fact, there are three of them. They don't talk with me and he didn't harm anybody. Woe is me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: When your grandson arrived, was he by himself or with other soldiers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: He was by himself. He -- he came in this military vehicle, what should we call it? It's a Campagnola, I think. But he had done nobody, anyone any harm. And in my neighbourhood, all the elderly people who used to live there with me, they have all died since.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And how long after the other soldiers left did your grandson arrive?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: I don't know how much time passed. Not much. They could not have reached the middle of the village by the time he arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And when your grandson arrived, were you still stripped at that point?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: I was unable to get dressed, and when I saw him coming with a rifle, I was scared even more and I didn't know how to get dressed. I was unable to do that. He had glasses on and I could not recognise him. And he told me, Just keep silent, Grandmother, and have patience. And I told him not to go and see who it was because there were more -- many more of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did you tell him what happened?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: I was so scared that I don't know really what I told him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Do you remember if he asked you what had happened when he saw you stripped?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: Of course he asked me. He saw me crying outside the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And did you talk to your grandson recently?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: No, no. I haven't spoken to him for a long time. He would perhaps come to visit me were it not for his mother and father who forbid him to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Do you know --

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: They do not visit me either.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Do you know why his mother and father forbade him to visit you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: Because they took everything I had. My livestock, two cows, two calves, 27 head of sheep, and I don't think they have the face to show up at my home.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Do you know whether your grandson is aware that you had mentioned his name your statement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: Of course he knows. That's why they're not coming to visit me. Of course I had to mention him if I was giving a statement, and there was nothing new in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: When you say "that's why they're not coming to visit me," is that something that they told you for a fact?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: Perhaps that's the reason why they're not coming to visit me. How should I know? The only thing I know is they're not coming, ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did they ever give you a reason as to why they were not coming to visit you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: Of course not. How would I know the reason why they're not coming, if they're not coming? Who would I talk to about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: In your statement you mention that your grandson wrote something on the wall of your house when he came. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: Yes. There's still that writing on -- which said, Do not touch the grandma.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me show you 65 ter 5496.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And that is at tab 3 in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can you please confirm that that is the -- that is the wall of your house that you see in front of you on that picture?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I don't know how well we can see on the screen but I will -- I can represent and if the Defence will agree that it -- what it says is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any way to agree on this because it's not well visible, but I think with some efforts --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I mean I can -- we can -- I can have --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't have anything on my picture here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, on the screen you can see that there are letters. I mean, the witness told us what, apparently, it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the issue is that, because she is illiterate, obviously she doesn't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I can have a declaration from the person who took the picture saying what it says. I can read it out for the record now and submit that later on if that's the Defence want to -- I can try to agree with them --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's it precisely. I'm illiterate and I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that, without the help of the witness, that the parties should come to agreement on what it -- what it says. At least I can decipher quite -- it starts with an N, then an E, then something difficult, and then I, R, A, U --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I believe it says, Do not touch, HV 142, and then occupied, zauzeto, on the last line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It would -- I would like just a minute to -- to deal with --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- everything but the last word I'm not able to make out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not bother the witness at this moment with it, because she couldn't help us out anyway. Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I would just like to tender 65 ter 5496, and I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P966, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P966 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mrs. Urukalo. I have no more questions for you. But other people may have some questions for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Urukalo, can you see me again, with the red robe, on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now further questions will you put to you by Defence counsel. They are not the same persons as you just saw. It's not again Mr. Hedaraly, although they are dressed in the same way. Could I inquire with Defence, Mr. Misetic. The first one of the Defence counsel who will put questions to you is Mr. Misetic. If you look at your screen you will see him, and he'll put questions to you. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. Urukalo.

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could have on the screen, please, 1D00-0410.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Urukalo, do you remember going to a notary public on the 15th of November, 1995, in which you authorised your son-in-law Dane Siklic and daughter Slavka Siklic to manage and dispose of some of your property?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: They dragged me to Sibenik to sign everything over. Whatever I had in my house. Poor me, they wanted to enjoy themselves at my expense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Some of the --

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: They did what nobody else did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... concrete mixer and your plough?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. A harrow drill which is attached to a tractor and a large mixer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... some of your livestock --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, the first portion of your question are missing when the previous translation continues. So would you take a pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I missed also the last two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Just for the record, the question at line 22 was: Did they also take your concrete mixer and your plough? The question at page 15, line 1, is: Did they also take some of your livestock?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So, Mrs. Urukalo, let me start again with the question about the livestock. Did they take some of your livestock as well?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: They took whatever I had. That's why they don't have the face to show up and come and see me. They told me that I would have 100 Deutschemarks, but I never saw any money from them, hell take them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Some of this livestock, did it include sheep, lambs, cows, calves, and pigs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: Two cows, two calves, two pigs that were as large as two wolves. What I regret the most is that they took four pigs from my kum. He should have gone to some other villages, not the villages -- not the village where he got married into.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't know if the Court would like me to translate "kum," but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that's a special relationship between --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Godfather or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- persons. Godfather, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Urukalo, when they took you to Sibenik, do you recall putting your fingerprint on a document there at the office of the notary public on the 15th of November, 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: Poor me, I did whatever they told me to do.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said that you did what they told to you do and then you added something. Could you please repeat what you then added.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. I repeated whatever they said to that notary public. And even if my children were to return, where would they go back to, when everything's been taken away from me? When you don't have a table and chairs in your own home, then you don't have anybody to keep you company, and he was received as a minister would be when he came to my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point I would ask that exhibit 1D00-0410 be given a number and I tender --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've gone through a lot of trouble.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D838.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D838 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could 1D00-0414, please. If we could go to page 2 in the English. First -- page 1 is fine, just so the Court can see it. This is a Defence witness statement taken of Mrs. Urukalo's grandson, Joska Siklic. If we could turn to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it your intention to tender this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, but I believe it is fair to put it to the witness, and if we have to call Mr. Siklic, then at least his testimony has been put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Urukalo, your grandson Joska gave a statement as well about what happened on the 6th of August --

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- and he says that he came on the 6th of August and that he and other members from the 6th Home Guard Regiment came to your hamlet and that you, the villagers, this is at paragraph 7, offered them what they had, mostly smoked ham, wine, and schnapps. Do you recall any of this, on the 6th of August?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: When he came, every day, until he was driven over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: When you say "he was driven over," do you mean that somebody drove him to your house everyday?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: He would come on his own. He had a car. He still has a car.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now at paragraphs 8 and 9 of his statement, he says: "During the time of my stay there, I didn't observe any mistreatment nor did anyone mention any mistreatment. "My grandmother never mentioned, particularly at that time, that she had been mistreated by any HV soldier. My grandmother never told me that she had been" --

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: Yes, now he can lie. I wouldn't have said that. They might have. Nobody would have said what they said had things not happened that way.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Poor me, to have had to come to see this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: He says: "My grandmother never told me that she had been forced by anyone to strip off her clothes and remain in her underwear or to play basketball with anyone."

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: I hope he was sane when he said that. What else could I tell you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] God forbid that that should happen to anyone. And it's up to them to say whatever they want, but they should leave me be, whatever might happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At paragraph 15 --

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: Got themselves into it and now they're trying to get out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At paragraph 15, he says: "My family took care of my grandmother throughout the time, and she authorised us to dispose of her property which she later certified at a notary public's office on 15 November 1995." Did your family take care of you from the time of Operation Storm until the 15th of November, 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: When they forced me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What did they force to you do?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness repeat --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were -- I -- they took out everything I had in my house and didn't bring anything when they would come to visit. By that token and by their standards, I could have ended up dead. And I can only wish that the same might happen to them, then they would see how I feel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. My last question is: Your grandson also said: "I didn't write anything on my grandmother's house, and I wouldn't know why I should have." Do you know who actually wrote something on the side of your house?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: Nobody else but him. There's no need to conceal or pretend in any way. Now, there you see how they're lying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They might even show up and set fire to it. I guess that's how it is going to end up, according to what he did to me so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, in light of the Court's previous rulings on Defence witness statements, we will not tender this exhibit, and I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Misetic. Could I inquire with the other Defence teams. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No need to re-examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mrs. Urukalo ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Urukalo, the Judges may have one or two questions for you as well. The first is Judge Gwaunza, who has one or more questions to you. Judge Gwaunza is a woman, and you'll see her on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you were dragged to the office of the notary public to sign over your property. My question is, could you not have refused to go and sign over your property?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: Well, poor me, I didn't want to go, but they took me over there. They could have taken me wherever they wanted to. They could do with me whatever they wanted. Shame on him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: So could you tell us when exactly they took away the property from your house?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: Whenever he came, he would take away something. I couldn't keep track of that, poor me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Urukalo, I have one question for you as well. We saw the picture of your house with barely visible words written on it, and it seemed to me that it had been covered by some kind of white paint. Have you seen that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: It was covered in whitewash. We whitewashed it, so that one wouldn't be able to see it anymore. Because nobody believed what the writing said any way, and whenever the soldiers came, it wasn't really worth anybody's while. Poor me, what have I come to live to see?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you done that yourself, whitewashing these words, and ...

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: I didn't do that. I don't know who did. Perhaps little Vuk did that, to cover it over, since Storm was over and done with. They could have killed my son. They did so many things to me that they could have done that as well. And my son, who did no harm to anyone, he was a driver and worked at a department store, as did my daughter. He even caught a pick-pocket in the department store. It was reported in the newspaper. He caught him at night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do your other children still see you and come to visit you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGINJA URUKALO
utterances.text: They don't visit me and how could I go over to see them? I -- I don't dare go around, and now I'm completely disgraced. I have nothing. I -- I was helping everybody, And my husband has been dead and buried for 23 years. I'm all alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Urukalo, I have no further questions for you, and since the -- Mr. Hedaraly also has no further questions for you, this concludes your testimony. Mrs. Urukalo, I do understand that it may not have been easy for you, at your age, to come and testify. I would like to thank you very much for having come and for having answered --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have to believe me when I tell you that I am sad. I am so aggrieved to have to spend my old age in such a way and there was no call for that. This did not need to happen. I should not have been mistreated as wretchedly as I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Urukalo, I again would like to thank you for coming and thank you for answering the questions that were put to you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This concludes your testimony. Then we'll disconnect --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the videolink at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I believe the witness that follows is here. He is present; Mr. Margetts is here as well. We can either proceed now or take a short break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we have had one hour of audience until now. Perhaps it would be better to have a bit of an earlier break so that we have a, more or less, natural re-start after the break. We will have a break and we resume at 25 minutes to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Buhin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Mikulicic, I look at the clock, and have in mind what we said yesterday to you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Buhin.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether I should say, accent-wise, Buhin or Buhin. I wouldn't like to mispronounce your name.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Buhin is correct. But as I grew up in Vukovar, I'm used to Buhin. It doesn't make any difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we finished with the issue of Grubori, and I should like to ask you another couple of questions in connection with Grubori. Tell us, did you know that after the report on the incident in Grubori, Romanic, the chief of the police administration, and Mr. Mihic, the chief of the Knin police station, attended the scene, or, rather went out into the terrain in order to find the location. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that they went out in the field. I only know that a patrol had been sent, which did not find the hamlet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You told us that you went to the UN base in order to conduct some talks there. Can you remember when was that exactly, on what day, in respect of the report on the Grubori, and we know we saw in the log yesterday that it was in the afternoon on the 25th. When was it that you went to the UN base?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 26th, the second day, in the morning, sometime around 9.00, my colleague Baric and I went to that base and got in touch with UN police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was actually the reason that prompted you to go there, you and your colleague Baric?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We got a report from them, that there were corpses in Grubori, and we assumed that they had been to the scene and that they could take us again to the place -- the scene of the event the easiest, to show us where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what was the result of this conversation? Did they confirm that they had indeed been to the scene of the event? What did you talk about?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They confirmed that they had been to the scene of the event and told us that they would gladly take us there, and so we agreed to meet sometime around 1300 hours, leaving, in other words, about three hours to organise the arrival of the investigating judge from Zadar and the on-site inspection team, so that we could all set out from Knin to Grubori together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: However, that never actually happened.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as I said, in the mean time, sometime around 1200 hours, I talked to Mr. Sacic, and Mr. Moric made that telephone call, and the idea was abandoned. Although, in the meantime, we had agreed with Mr. Cetina that everything would indeed be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for these answers.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the Defence counsel please speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Mikulicic. You're again invited to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will try to, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I ask you one thing in relation to your last answer, Mr. Buhin. What idea was abandoned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This agreement, to the effect that the investigating judge and an on-site investigation team would arrive in Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the idea was abandoned that an investigation team would arrive and be sent to the place . And at the same time, you said: "Although, in the meantime, we had agreed with Mr. Cetina that everything would indeed be carried out." On the one hand, you say the idea was abandoned, but we agreed that everything would be carried out. How do I have to understand that answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, we -- I had agreed with Mr. Cetina that the investigating judge and his team would come around 1200 hours. That they would come around 1200 hours when Mr. Moric called and told us that I and Mr. Baric -- actually he told me that they were not meddle in the work of the police. I stopped all actions of the police and I never got in touch again with either the UN police or with anybody else in connection with that particular procedure. That is what I meant when I said that we abandoned the agreed job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So on from that moment, you say the idea was abandoned to send an investigation team. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. From that moment, from the moment when Mr. Moric called me on the telephone, I no longer worked on anything in connection with the event in the village of Grubori and no longer liaised with the UN police. What happened afterwards, I did not follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So whether the idea of sending an investigation team was abandoned or not is, you say, I stepped out, I had got nothing to do with it anymore, so whether that idea was abandoned or not, is that within your knowledge or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Actually, I didn't know -- what I meant -- I said we abandoned the idea about a meeting with the UN police and the going of the regular police, of the uniformed police to the scene of the event. All the other agreements remained at the level of any deals between Mr. Cetina and the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... please proceed, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you said that the idea was abandoned, you meant the idea for you to be engaged in that particular work, and after talking with Mr. Moric, that idea was abandoned in view of his instructions that you should steer clear of the crime police with the regular police. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for the explanation. One question in that regard. Did you know that that day when the incident in Grubori took place, a meeting had been called between the UN with the locals in the school in Plavno, because of certain security problems in the Plavno valley. Were you informed of that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember, but I probably wasn't because I would have remembered that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Buhin, in your statement, you said that - and that is page 5, the penultimate section in the Croatian version, P963, i.e., page 6, the second paragraph in the English version. You said that you learned later that the killings in Grubori had not been properly processed as a criminal case. Can you elaborate a bit on this. When was this "later" that you learned about it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only learned about it when I returned to work in the Ministry of the Interior, in Zagreb, talking with my colleagues from the crime police who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But were you aware or are you aware today that, in fact, the investigation into the Grubori case is still an open case in the Sibenik prosecution's office?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not follow those issues, and I have no knowledge whatsoever about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Further, in your statement, Mr. Buhin, you refer to killings in the village of Gosic and you stated that you personally were, together with Mr. Romanic and other people, at the scene of the event. This incident, together with the incident in Varivode, was the subject of a joint investigation of the military police, the crime police, and the crime police of the Ministry of the Interior. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that incident, but as regards the details of the investigation, I don't know. I know there was an on-site investigation but I do not recall all the particulars, in terms of who participated, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We have already seen exhibits in that regard. I should like to refer you to P802, which -- from which it stems that the -- there was an Operative Action Varivode organised which specifies the relevant tasks of the military police and of the uniformed police. In this connection I should like to ask you this. You said that nobody called you to testify in connection with the Gosic killings. You were not an eye-witness to those events, were you not?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Together with the uniformed police, I looked for the scene of the event and we came to the scene of the event. We secured it in keeping with the rules of service, rules of procedure of the regular police, and everything else was done by workers of the crime police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In other words, you did not participate in the crime processing of the scene?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Will you agreed with me, Mr. Buhin, that it is not at all customary for a police force member to be called to testify in a court case, if (a), he is not an eye-witness to the -- to the actual event or has some knowledge which is of relevance to the procedure. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So the fact that were not called to testify in an event with the Varivode and Gosici killings is not something out of the ordinary, it's not something strange; right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did not surprise me at all. I didn't see the need for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I should like to refer now to your statement in which you stated that the Croatian government entrusted the police, through the Ministry of the Interior, to protect people and property. Do you remember having stated that? That is --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is basic police work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: For reference, this is page 7 in the English text. It is the third paragraph. You told us in your testimony that the police had problems because of the shortage of people, the booby-traps in the field, in the terrain, because of its unfamiliarity with the terrain, because the police officers were not sufficiently experienced and trained. So that the police obviously had to set some priorities for itself in that terrain, am I wrong or is this consistent with your view?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, definitely. In view of the numbers and technical and other capacities, that is exactly what we had to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, what were these priorities in?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The priorities were to secure vital facilities which were in the area, to secure facilities in which police officers were accommodated, the facilities of the police station and police administration themselves, to establish check-points in order to put under supervision the main roads, firstly. And as regards the rest of the policemen, of which there were only a few indeed, they were used for patrolling and they would patrol -- they would patrol according to specifically-assigned tasks and not generally, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you speak about vital facilities, does that also include ecclesiastical buildings, cultural historical buildings, industrial facilities and such buildings?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely because it was precisely in Kistanje that we found an undamaged monastery, and we posted on permanent guard ten policemen there to see to the security of that facility. Also, there was a school in Kistanje which I believe was also undamaged. There we posted guards, policemen. In Kistanje, we also guarded a factory, I don't remember which one, and a series of other important buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: To your recollection, in doing this, did you come across depots of military equipment that had been left behind after the troops of the so-called army of the Serbian Krajina had left?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not come across any depot. We just came across a proving ground that was used by Martic's militia. It was partly devastated. There was traces of damage and of looting there, but when we came there we posted policemen there who sought to protect that facility as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that in the monastery which was the subject of your protection a certain amount of ammunition and explosions were found?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In the introduction we mentioned what the basic duty was of coordinators and it was basically to implement this policy, if you agree with me, the policy of the Republic of Croatia which was assigned to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now just for a moment, please, move into private session because we are going to show a document -- exhibit, rather, P501, which was exhibited under seal. So P501, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Are you agree with me that through these instructions, the idea you referred to was operationalized or implemented where the government entrusted MUP with the task of protecting property and individuals?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These were the fundamental tasks that were regulated as well by the Law on Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you at any point in time in the course of your duty come to learn that the government of the Republic of Croatia through the Ministry of the Interior was taking any steps or actions that were aimed at concealing crimes of any sort, or did you come across anything that would indicate something of the sort?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, did you ever officially communicate with General Markac on any particular case?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never communicated with him orally. We only met in the ministry offices or would come across each other. I knew him by sight and we never communicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Buhin, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Misetic, who is counsel for Mr. Gotovina, at least if he receives the furniture he needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Buhin.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to start on a topic yesterday -- that you spoke of yesterday. Do you recall you were asked by Mr. Kay as to whether Minister Jarnjak had ever been in Knin and your response was that, as far as you knew, he was not in Knin after Operation Storm while you were there. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Were you present when the plaque was put up in Knin on the 6th of August for the police administration, Knin?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only remember that -- not on the 6th, two or three days Mr. Moric arrived and brought the plaques that we put up. I can't remember, but I believe that the plaque bearing the inscription "police administration" was already put up by the time I had come there, by the time I arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, I would like to show the witness the video at D227.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] "Mr. Chief, please allow me to hand over to you the signboard bearing the inscription 'Ministry of the Interior, Republic of Croatia, Ministry of the Interior, police administration Knin.' It is provided by the constitutional Law on Ethnic Minorities of the Republic of Croatia that Knin should have a district, Kotar, and accordingly, the police administration should be established in Knin. "Since, according to the aforementioned law, an assembly has not been legitimately elected yet and upon this assembly's proposal the chief should be appointed by the government of the Republic of Croatia, I hereby appoint you the acting chief until the elections take place here and the assembly is elected, whereupon the assembly will propose to the government of the Republic of Croatia, its chief. Until then, I am assigning to you the task to perform any activities provided for by the constitution of the Republic of Croatia and the laws of the Republic of Croatia to establish civilian authority in Knin and in the area of your police administration. In your area of responsibility, you are linked up with the police administration in Zadar. "Congratulations."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. No. Yes. Congratulations have been translated, yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, do you recall being present for that ceremony?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I most certainly was not. This was probably in the morning hours of the 6th of August before Mr. Baric and I arrived Knin. That's why I don't recall this event.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Is it the case then that Mr. Romanic came to Knin -- was already in Knin by the time you had arrived?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. And he took over from Mr. Jarnjak, the plaque bearing the inscription "the police administration."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'd also like to talk to you about this issue that you discussed with Mr. Margetts about when civilians started to return to Knin. And first what I'm going to do is show you a series of documents, and after I have shown you a series of documents, I'm going to ask you a few questions on the basis of those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could have Exhibit P352, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Baric [sic], this is an report, a situation report from UN Sector South in Knin, on the 6th of August, at 2030. You can see that on the cover page. And if we go to page 6 of this report in the English, please, this would be point F.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this stage can I just confirm that this is not part of the materials that were disclosed to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It should have been. We'll check on that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so and meanwhile you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At paragraph F, the UN reported on the 6th in -- towards the middle of that paragraph: "More civilians including cars with Split licence plates are seen in Knin, and a sense of normalcy is returning." And now -- that's on the 6th at 2030.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could now have Exhibit P806, please. I'm advised by my case manager, Your Honour, that it has been disclosed to the Prosecution. It's item 50 on the list that was disclosed to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While Mr. Margetts is seeking to verify, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, this is a report of the European Community Monitoring Mission. It is dated the 8th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 2, please, of this document, under section 4 a.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: On the 8th of August, the European Community Monitoring Mission wrote: "Locals and HV continue looting on a large scale with a convoy of looters was seen going empty and returning full from these towns. DPs are already returning to their former homes." That's on the 8th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Registrar, if we could go to Exhibit P933, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And on that very first page, right above the section that starts "military situation," there's a paragraph -- and this is a European Community report from Knin dated 9 August 1995. And that paragraph says: "It seems like Knin, for the first time, is becoming a big tourist attraction. Extensive traffic was recorded on the main road between Knin and Drnis." And if we could go to the next page of this document, please. Under "humanitarian matters," towards the middle of that section, with respect to Drnis, it says: "We saw the same development in Drnis. A lot of civilians are in the city, and it seems they are looking for property that belonged to them previously." Now, Mr. Buhin, you were asked questions about when civilians started to return to the area, and I've now shown you three documents that were admitted into evidence by the Prosecution from both UN and European community sources which indicate that civilians began to return in Knin and in the former Sector South within days of the end of Operation Storm. Is that consistent with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What I remember the most clearly is that most of the civilians came in with the arrival of the first train from Zagreb. Thereafter, a regular train line was introduced and civilians started flowing in Knin both from Zagreb and Split. It's difficult to remember all the details, but according to these reports, certain civilians who were in possession of some sort of passes, went past check-points or travelled roads that were not under the control of the police. This was a rather large area, and the locals were aware of both main roads and side roads. Roads that were not under police control were widely travelled along, and the UN police monitored the situation and recorded it, and, of course, there were such cases, most certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'll get to the issue of the train in a moment, but I also wanted to ask you, these reports talk about displaced persons returning to their former homes. And they also talk about, in the instance of Drnis, the report mentions that to the European Union Monitoring Mission, it seemed that these civilians were looking for property that belonged to them previously. Was that a common occurrence in the area, of displaced people coming back into the region and looking for their own personal property; and what problems, if any, did that cause for the police in terms of prevention of looting?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a common occurrence, indeed. Those -- these were individuals who tried to reach their properties as soon as possible, and whatever they were able to salvage from there, they took along with them to the refugee centres. Problems were experienced by -- at the check-points because they were unable to prove that what they took along was indeed their property. To counter that, they tried to use some side roads, less travelled roads, in order to get past, and this constituted a great problem for the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If someone at a check-point, a displaced person or refugee, told a police officer at a check-point that the goods that were in the car now were, in fact, goods that had belonged to them and had been stolen from them during the occupation period, how would a police officer know whether that person had, in fact, stolen the goods or that they belonged to that person; and what steps would a police officer typically take?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Police officers were not able to tell at all whether the goods were, in fact, stolen or had previously belonged to that individual. Nobody was authorised to issue citizens with a receipt against which they could take such goods outside of the area. Most often, individuals were recommended that they should remain close to their property in order to protect it, and it was only later that they were able to establish, if, indeed, some of the goods were stolen or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. With respect to the train, I will put it to you that I think the parties in this case agree that the date of the freedom train, when President Tudjman came to Knin, was the 26th of August, 1995. I would like to show you now a video from the 15th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, this is 1D00-0423.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "Sasa Kopljar: Up next is Knin and our colleague Denis Latin. Good evening, Denis. "Denis Latin: Good evening, Sasa. Good evening to Croatia from Knin. "Sasa Kopljar: It is the Assumption of the Virgin Mary. Has this holiday been celebrated in Knin that had been liberated only ten days ago? "Denis Latin: I must say that it was remarkable in Knin today. We estimate that somewhere between two to three thousand people visited Knin today. I think that the image is very telling, so let's take a look at the TV feature. "More than 500 refugee people from Knin have arrived on the first train out of Split to Knin, and the Assumption of the Virgin Mary has also given a chance for others who -- for everyone else to make a true fete on the streets of the town. "After the Holy Mass in the torched church of Saint Ante, most of the Knin townsmen proceeded to their homes determined never to leave them again."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, there you saw a train that arrived from Split to Knin on the 15th of August, which appeared to have many civilians on it. Do you recall that, in fact, train service from Split was carrying civilians into Knin well before President Tudjman's freedom train came on the 26th of August?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am in a dilemma here because according to the footage, one can see that the train service had been placed into operation earlier on. I believed that it had been made operational only when President Tudjman travelled on the train to Knin, and it's only now that I'm able to see that this was the case even before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, these people that were on the train that had come in from Split, it says there were about 500 people on the train. The reporter makes as reference to 2.000 to 3.000 people that were in Knin on that day. It wasn't the case, was it, that all of those people needed a special pass to be able to enter Knin?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such a multitude of people could not have been issued with passes, to begin with. It is true that they got in without a pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender into evidence the video at 1D00-0423.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D839.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D839 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will just take this opportunity to indicate that the document was in the binder but obscured. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, I'd like to go to Exhibit D661, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, what we have on the screen is something called a Work Order from the 6th Benkovac police station. The date is 11th to 12th September, 1995. There's a patrol identified and the name Stefan Ljutic. First, can you explain what is a Work Order for a patrol?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the customary form, namely, Work Order which every police officer or patrol is given before they proceed to carry out their assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we look at this Work Order, the tasks that were given to this patrol, the third task from the bottom, it says: "Perform verification and inspection of any suspicion persons and vehicles (vehicles with HV licence plates in particular) and deliver compulsory Official Notes." Then it says: "Persons who are detected carrying objects and items shall be handed over to the police station for criminal processing." If we could turn the page, please. This is an report section of this work order, then, which appears to be the actual report of the patrol as to what they had done pursuant to the work order. If you read what this patrol said that they did on the 12th of September, it says: "At 2030 hours on the road between Biljane Gornje and Atlagica Kula, we came across Ostric, Pero," gives his date of birth, "dressed in a HV uniform and driving a stolen vehicle, type Zastava 750. He was taken in at this police station for further processing. In cooperation with military police officials, the vehicle was seized according to an appropriate confirmation." According to this Work Order, the police were in fact able to stop suspicious vehicles including vehicles that had HV plates on them. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The individual drafting assignments and giving assignments to patrols was probably lacking in experience, because that person could not have given an assignment to the civilian police to check vehicles bearing licence plates of the Croatian army. That's number one. Number two, at the back we can see that the police acted properly because they pulled over a vehicle, which was of the type Zastava 750, and it was a civilian vehicle. They were able to establish that it was driven by a person in military uniform, and together with the military police, further crime investigation was undertaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, so it's safe to say that someone who was a Croatian army member, in uniform, could be stopped by the police in the commission of a criminal act and taken to the local MUP police station to be turned over to the military police. That was the proper procedure. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go, please, to Exhibit D97.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is a report sent by Minister Jarnjak on the 2nd of October, 1995, to the state prosecutor, Mr. Hranjski.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Could we go to page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: These are statistics for the period of 22 August to 2 October 1995. And it talks about by police administration, the statistics for various types of crime. And then if we go to the section which talks about the perpetrator profile. For Zadar-Knin, it talks about 192 on-site investigations, known perpetrators were identified --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: One, moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this the document where we earlier had the problem that the three --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's what I'm checking, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm told the correct version is in e-court. It just needs to be linked to the translation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We have visited --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, we have, Your Honour. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- this problem before, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In the Croatian version, sir, you can see that it identifies the perpetrators in Zadar-Knin, 28 members of the HV, 194 civilians, and 1 abuse of uniform. Now, in fact the police could identify and investigate HV -- perpetrators of crimes even if they happened to turn out to be HV members, correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot claim that, because if it was established that the perpetrator was a member of the Croatian army, the military police would be called in and they would continue processing the case. Perhaps in some instances, due to professional reasons, or some other issues, they would work on it together, to see what the perpetrator had committed as a member of the army and what as a civilian person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's go Exhibit D809 then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am asked to ask for your permission to make the change in Exhibit D97 to replace the English translation currently there with the corrected English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is even welcomed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is a criminal report filed by Mr. Kardum, dated 1 September 1995. And if you look at this page, sir, it is a criminal complaint filed against a Nino Starcevic, who is identified by Mr. Kardum as a soldier listed in the military register of Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we turn the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If you read through that, it appears that Mr. Starcevic was involved in the theft of a vehicle which was seized from him and a criminal report filed. Now, in fact, Ministry of the Interior officials could file criminal reports against persons they identified as being members of the HV. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that -- I cannot claim that because according to what I know, all such processing was to have been done by the military police. But I might be wrong there, because I'm not an expert on the duties of the crime police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can we go to Exhibit D486, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this is a report by Cedo Romanic dated 21 September 1995. I'd ask to you read through that, please, and then tell me when you've finished reading it.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. This is an incident where a policeman at a check-point fired two rounds from a machine-gun into a vehicle driven by staff commander Miroslav Lucin because he attempted to drive away from the check-point. Mr. Romanic, in the letter, indicates that the use of force was appropriate. Do you agree that a police officer could, in fact, use force to detain a HV commander, if force was necessary, to prevent the commission of a crime?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, that was acceptable. Today, when communication resources are much more favourable, I'm sure that the police would act in a quite different way, that they would try follow that vehicle up to the point where it would be possible to stop the vehicle and do their police duty. It was early on in the early days of the war. There were still -- people were trigger-happy. The police did that with a reason in order to stop him. And it was to be expected that such an aggressive person who said to -- who said he was a member of the police could perhaps act in an even graver manner, so that is why that particular action was acceptable at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, the issue of forged certificates --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, could we get an answer from the witness what -- on what apparently was your question. It was not what kind of force you would use against a person under certain circumstances, but I understood your question to be whether the witness could comment on a police officer acting against a military person even in a command position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- at line 17 I thought he answered that, but if it needs more clarification, that's fine. Page 46, line 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But I understood the answer of the witness mainly to be what kind of force would you use under circumstances, would you follow him, et cetera. Whereas I understood your question to be: Could you explain how someone who is just a member of the civilian police could act against someone who was clearly a -- in a military command position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That apparently was the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And there is an issue that arises from this document as to who, in fact, the action was directed against, given that there were two people of differing status, and so it would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But let's not -- let's not discuss this in the presence of the witness what -- so if you put a question and if the witness takes half a minute to answer that question, of course, the Chamber would highly appreciate if the answer is, first of all, related to your question, then also assists the Chamber in better understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'd -- if this document is the exemplar that the witness is directing his mind to, then I'd ask for a characterization of the content of this document, rather than a partial characterization of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I asked him to read the document, so I don't know how much better characterization he could get than to tell him to read it for himself. But if we could ask him to unplug his microphone [sic], because I don't think there is an issue here as to who the real perpetrator is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it clearly says, certainly in the Croatian version and I think in the English, but let me say it again. It says: Staff commander Miroslav Lucin came into oral conflict with the aforementioned policemen, offending them and preventing them in exercising their duty.
