Then he sat in the driver's seat, aiming to drive away." And in the Croatian you will note that there wasn't a period between the "their duty" and the "then he sat ..." It is all one sentence speaking of commander Miroslav Lucin. So I have no doubt that the sentence is referring to the commander and that that use of the word "he" is not ambiguous in the original, but if that is the issue ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Our problem is that this is a problematic document to use for this particular question. The car is driven by Dragomir Zepina, who is a person under the -- or a civilian, and it's -- initially the co-driver is the military police staff commander. So it is a situation where we have a joint action of forces against persons representing different bodies. It is not a situation that's as clear as a specific action alone by a civilian policeman against military perpetrator, so we prefer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, it is clear -- if you look at the story, there is a car and what I know from cars a Moskovich 1500 might well be a civilian car driven by someone of whom we do not -- we don't know. Mr. Zepina is not described as either civilian or --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We have a division --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Let me see. They're taken to two different places at a later stage which --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. As we see it, what we have here is we have the military police and civilian police acting together against a civilian and against a military perpetrator, and if a question is put indicating the joint action against the diverse persons, then we see that as appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I mean -- with all due respect, he can characterize it in redirect any way he wishes. What it talks about is the joint action once the both of them were taken to the police station in Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I see the point Mr. Margetts is making. We see a car arriving at a check-point, apparently with two persons in it, one, if you read it carefully, most likely a civilian; the other one certainly a military person, a commander. Then action is taken, and from the action taken there is a possibility that this was a joint check-point because it said the official of the 6th police station, Benkovac, and the 72nd Battalion of military police Benkovac operated on the side. Now I take it that Mr. Margetts reads it this as on the side, the check-point, which of course is a matter of interpretation as well. So what Mr. Margetts is putting here, that this may have been a joint check-point, where most likely one civilian and certainly one military person arrive in what seems to be, at first sight, a civilian vehicle, and they then take action. And Mr. Margetts's problem apparently is that you introduced this to the witness as an example of how the ordinary police, civilian police, could take action against a military commander. Where -- have I characterized --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, absolutely. That is precisely the point. And the second point is this, that it's not clear at what time or when it is ascertained that this individual has any association with the military at all. I don't see a reference to military uniform; I see a driver who appears to be a civilian in a civilian vehicle. That's all I see here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's not what it says, Judge, and if I may respond --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- because there's been a lot communication. I think there is misinterpretation of what was said. I don't think there's any reference to a joint check-point. What we have in evidence already is once the person is detained, they also could have called in the military police after blowing out the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At sight --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- called him -- I'm reading the Croatian version which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which line exactly are you reading?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says -- the third paragraph. It is translated as operated on the site. In the original it says, at the crime scene, the following persons or officials took action. So there an a difference between they were operating generally on the site and here's a crime scene now, there's an HV member, the car tire has been blown out, and the HV military police and the civilian police arrived on the scene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is it also an interpretation. What we have now down is the following. We asked the witness to read a document which at least, I mean, three, if I could say, trained lawyers are having quite some dispute about --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could make one other point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you'd --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The fact of the matter is, I first showed him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: --- if you could just let me finish for one second. At least disagreements on what the document tells us exactly. Now to ask the witness to read it and without knowing how he interprets what is written here, it might be a -- it might cause a lot of confusion as whether we're talking about the same thing. Whether he has not read something, he has read the Croatian version, read something totally different from what I read, from what you read, from what Mr. Margetts read and that's a matter that should be avoided. I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: While I understand Mr. Margetts's position, obviously we think his position is wrong. And I did put it to the witness prior to this document, the work order which said specifically to the police in this particular police station to stop HV vehicles including vehicles with HV licence plates on them. I take it then to the next step. Now the fact that the witness says, Somebody wrote that order who didn't know what they were doing, is something that you can give weight to at some point. We're going to argue something different. I understand Mr. Margetts wants to now dissect this document, but I would be happy to put it to the witness, since is he a policeman, to interpret whether he thinks the policemen here would -- my question is, you shot out the tire of a car driven by a commander in the Croatian army. That's it. Could he use force to shoot out a tire of a car driven by a member of the Croatian army. If they, in redirect, want to say, well, yes, they could shoot out car tires driven by commanders of civilian -- in civilian cars but not military cars, fine. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But that needs a level of analysis which I think we should not require from a witness, because I don't know whether the witness feels free to say, well -- to describe all circumstances in which this would be acceptable or not acceptable would take us half an hour. I would not mind if you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There is an issue in dispute, though, between the parties, just so the Chamber's aware of it. Their position is that anybody wearing a military uniform could not be stopped by the police. That has been their position to date. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- my question --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: -- it is probably better that we characterize our position --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... why I'm bringing the issue up. If they're going to stipulate, then, that the fact that the someone was wearing a military uniform did not mean that force could not be used against them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under no circumstances --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- yes, then I'll walk away from it. But if that isn't something they're going to dispute, then I want to put it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now Mr. Margetts has an opportunity to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: The first thing I'd say is our position in relation to the use of military uniforms doesn't -- is not necessarily relevant to this document because there is no reference in this document to whether or not there is a military uniform being used. There's no reference in this document that would suggest, apart from the person subsequently being identified as a member of the military, that the people knew at the time the action was taken that they were a member of the military. As to our position in relation to the use of military uniforms, there's substantial evidence and it is quite clear from the contemporaneous documents how the fundamental police in fact acted at that time, and I think this witness has given substantial evidence in relation to that. And that's the issue that -- that needs to be resolved, and I think that that document confounds the issue and potentially leads -- misleads the witness and doesn't, in fact, bring to light any evidence that would be relevant to that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with all due respect, the fact that he takes a particular view of a document doesn't mean that I can't put it to a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: He did it with his diary. He is putting other people's diaries to this witness when he didn't have any concern about such matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, the Chamber assesses that the risk of confusion with this document in relation to the matter you are raising with the witness is too large to continue to do that. This is not to keep you off in any way from dealing with the substance you want to raise but not on the basis of a document which leaves so many questions as far as what it actually, in factual terms, describes. So, therefore, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, in order to stop someone in the commission of a crime, including a member of the HV, if the military police was not with the police, the regular police at the scene of the crime being committed, the police was authorised to use force to stop members of the HV from committing crimes. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I put it to him if in this document it turned out such-and-such would that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's stay away from the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yesterday a few hypothetical questions were put, I did not encourage to do this anymore, but if you would clearly and hypothetically describe a situation then we'd like to hear the answer of the witness. Then at least the confusion is gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So under those circumstances, exceptionally, I would allow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At a check-point -- at some point -- let me take a foundational question first. Are you aware that at some point around the 15th of September, the joint check-points with the military police stopped and that it was just the MUP that was controlling the check-points?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when this was done, but I do know that it was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If the MUP alone was operating a check-point, and a member of the HV driving a civilian vehicle refused to stop at a MUP check-point, it's true, is it not, that the MUP officers were authorised to use force, if necessary, to stop that person at the check-point?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true. The more so as the police had no way of knowing what was being transported in the vehicle and what the intention was. So the vehicle had to be stopped at all costs and a check made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to a new topic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, of course, it came to my mind if a civilian vehicle approaches a check-point, how to know that there's a military person in it. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If the person -- if a civilian vehicle approaches a check-point, all persons driving such a vehicle had to stop at the check-point, even someone wearing a military uniform. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the people would have to produce their IDs to show -- for it to be seen, whether they were indeed military staff or just persons in military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if that ID proves to the officer at the check-point that the person is a member of the HV, and, at the same time, the officer sees goods in the car that he believes are stolen, that officer was authorised to detain that member of the HV on the spot, or to take him to the local police station, and then to await the arrival of the military police for further processing. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, on the issue of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, one moment. I don't know when our next break is going to be so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I forgot to look at the clock, which is -- let me just ... we started a bit late. I think we should take a break within the next ten minute, approximately, somewhere within the next ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're invited to choose a suitable moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, now let's talk about these certificates, I think you called them in your statements, that you believe may have been forged. Do you recall the testimony about that issue?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: First, did you personally ever see a military vehicle carrying goods which you believed to be stolen, you personally?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you personally ever witness the military police allowing a military vehicle through with a forged certificate?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was never present at any such event.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How -- so I assume, then, that what you're referring to is something that was reported to you by subordinate police officers?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I came to know that, I personally, from my conversations with police officers who manned check-points. They saw a -- lorries bearing HV labels going past check-points. There were stories about goods that were not intended, in fact, for the purposes of the HV, but they only remained what they were at the time, namely, rumours, because it was very difficult to pinpoint what exactly the term "for the purposes of the Croatian army" meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, you as -- at your level and your subordinates had no ability to actually verify those rumours. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Were you or your subordinate police officers aware that HV military vehicles were being used to provide logistical support to all sorts of civilian governmental -- typically civilian governmental activities in the newly liberated area?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot claim with certainty that we knew of that. There were assumptions of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You were there in the region. Is it fair to say that the institution with the most logistical capabilities, the institution within the Croatian government with the most logistical capabilities at that time in that area was the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody else was able to pull that off at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So the army would have been involved in things like clearing roads. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The army was involved in cleaning up the cities from the debris that had been caused by military action. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was primarily within the domain of the civilian protection, but the army equipment was mostly used for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You testified earlier that you believed that General Cermak was a -- had as one of his roles to restore -- restore the infrastructure in the area. Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood the role of General Cermak to be an all-encompassing one, to assist in every activity geared toward restoring normalcy to that town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And that would include assisting the civilian government in the tasks that it couldn't fulfil at that time, due to lack of logistics. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And were you aware that, General Cermak, in trying to assist in this -- assist the civilian authorities, had at his disposal trucks and various other items to assist the civilian government in restoring life back in that region?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only members of the army had larger quantities of vehicles and lorries at their disposal. The civilian authorities had far fewer of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So what was actually being transported in those vehicles, your police officers wouldn't know unless they were themselves able to check what was actually being transported and for what reason. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My last question -- questions to you, sir, are concerning Exhibit D48, please. As we pull this up on the screen, would you agree with me that if military police personnel at check-points were allowing HV trucks with looted goods to pass through the check-points, that that would be a criminal act being committed by the HV military police at those check-points. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, on -- in his letter to Mr. Lausic, on the 17th of August, Mr. Moric writes about various problems that they're having with the HV. And Mr. Margetts asked you about this letter and said -- asked you whether some of the things in this letter were things that you had been reporting up to Zagreb, and you agreed with him that that was the case. Now, if, in fact, it was a problem that the military police at check-points was essentially aiding and abetting military personnel in looting goods out of the area, that would have been something that you reported to Mr. Moric so he could refer it on to Mr. Lausic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Buhin. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, just -- I have a very short re-examination, five to ten minutes, I hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Your suggestion is to continue --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and then to adjourn for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, the Chamber prefers to have a break now. We might have some questions as well. And that sometimes triggers new questions from the other parties and then we would have to stop anyhow. So, therefore, we will take a break - I have difficulties in seeing the clock - we will have a break and we'll resume at 20 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I heard B/C/S on channel 4. I don't hear it anymore, so the problem will be resolved. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, if I could please produce D233 on the screen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, another problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll just repeat that. Mr. Registrar, if I could please produce D233 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin. Mr. Buhin, yesterday evening, Mr. Mikulicic asked you about the duties of the civilian protection sanitation teams. And, in particular, you addressed the issue of the removal of explosives and very briefly you touched on the forensic technicians and the role of the sanitation teams. What I've produced before you is order of the 5th of August, 1995, and if you could just read that for me. It's from Zdravko Zidovec. And it's -- deals with hygiene and sanitation measures. So if you just read that for me and indicate to me when you've read through the document.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Buhin. Just a very brief question. Have you ever seen that order before or were the matters set out in that order communicated to you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen that. I only came to know that this was the way it was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And so the procedure set out at items 1 to 4 are consistent with your knowledge as to how the sanitation teams carried out their duty.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. That's the way it should have been done. Now, whether this was observed in all the cases is something I cannot confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Buhin. Now I'd like to move on to another topic and that is today Mr. Misetic addressed with you the issue of the return of civilians to the area. And in your answer to one of his questions you stated that civilians in possession of some sort of passes would pass through the check-points. Now, my question to you is: At that time, in August 1995, were you concerned about the possible presence of terrorists or those who opposed Croatian control entering the territory?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure what that has to do with my cross-examination, the presence of terrorists, and I also think it mischaracterizes certainly portions of his testimony concerning these passes. I think he clarified that after -- concerning whether these people that I showed him had passes. I think the answer was quite the opposite of what is being represented here. And I also don't know that I asked him about terrorists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. It is about control of people returning or at least moving around to the area, and you may proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Buhin, the -- the question is: At that time, in August 1995, were you concerned about the possible presence of terrorists or those who opposed Croatian control entering the territory?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course we were concerned about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And that concern, is that one of the reasons that -- that passes were issued, civilians were registered and care was taken in respect of those matters?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And so would it be correct, then, to say that part of the role of the fundamental police was to monitor and to know who was on the territory?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Where persons were asked to produce their IDs, one had to establish whether that individual had been registered during or after combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And at the check-points that -- you made efforts to do that -- and in the territory, generally, you made efforts to establish who was present?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also at the check-points one had to monitor whoever was coming in or going out, and the patrols in the field asked suspicious individuals to present their IDs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Buhin. That concludes my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just short recross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What we often do is that we now put in the questions of the Judges, so that you have a kind of -- if they trigger any need. Mr. Buhin, Judge Gwaunza has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: Yes, if I could take you back to your statement, page 5 of the English version, and paragraph 4. I'm not sure what paragraph that would be in the other version. You said in that paragraph, in the middle, that: "After the military had liberated Knin, some of them continued into Bosnia. On their return, these soldiers started looting and burning." My question is: When did they return; and are you aware of any action that was taken to stop the looting and the burning?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the early days it was almost impossible to control that, due to the large numbers of individuals in HV uniforms, due to a very scarce presence of the police. As a result of all that, it was almost impossible to control such occurrences. It was only ten or more days later that stricter control was applied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: Thank you. The first part of my question was when did they return?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies, can you repeat that, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: Yes. I had asked -- because you said in your statement that after the military had liberated Knin, some of the military personnel continued into Bosnia and then you said "on their return," and I'm assuming that you are referring to -- to those military personnel you said on their return, these soldiers started looting and burning, and my question was when did they return?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't pinpoint the exact time. It was certainly 5, 10 or 15 days later. I can't be more precise than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I have another question relating to the last paragraph on -- on the same page. Towards the very end of that paragraph. And here you are talking of police officers retiring, and you said: "Some of them retired because of mistakes that they had made." And the question I have is: Do you know what mistakes those were?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I was able to learn, they failed to apply measures that they were able to apply and should have applied at the time. It involved the areas of Glina and Petrina; however, I'm not quite certain of the details relating to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GWAUNZA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Kinis has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Buhin, first I would like to ask you a general question and, namely, could you please explain difference between police log-book and criminal record register book? And how it was created.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The log-book of events is kept in the duty service of every police station and police administration. Entries are made according to the date and time of information received, the contents of the information, and, under a separate column, what measures were taken and when. The criminal record register book is quite a different document kept in the offices of the crime police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Based on this, your answer, I would like to -- to clarify the following issue. How you could determine whether accident which is reported to the police contains elements of crime or not, if you did not commit any examination of incident place?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could not be determined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: But then the question how -- how -- what kind of procedure is that you should report that this is -- this particular incident is a crime and this particular incident is not a crime?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: After a report was made, or any other sort of information received about a criminal offence having been committed, a patrol would be deployed or a constable of the basic police force to check up on that. Only after the information was checked up on by a police officer, further steps were taken depending on whether it was established that this indeed involved a criminal offence or whether it was merely a hoax, a false report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: And following this issue, I would like to ask registrar to bring up your statement and page 4 in English and first paragraph on the top. In this paragraph, you mentioned: "I would get information about crimes that were committed every day. And we would send out police to the scene, if it was possible, and report the facts," et cetera. But my question is, could you interpret or explain to Chamber what does it mean your passage "if it was possible"?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As these were conditions immediately after combat in an unfamiliar terrain, to the policemen that is, and mined terrain at that, there were instances when that was difficult or practically impossible to go out and attend the scene immediately after having received information. Sometimes we needed to carry out additional steps to ensure the presence of a de-mining team and of persons familiar with the terrain, and that is the kind of thing that I meant when I said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Yes. But I am understand this that there is some circumstances or some -- some reasons which may hinder work of police, and police are not able to react immediately. But would it mean -- or if I'm not correct, please correct me, but if I'm understood from your question, would it mean that police not interfere in such situations at all?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police always sought to verify information. We never gave up. The question was only whether it was only possible to do so immediately or after having taken other measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: But it means that you can confirm here and ensure Tribunal that in all -- in all situations where reports was received that some kind of criminal activities was taken, police actions followed. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: And then the next question. Regarding -- regarding Exhibit D49, and particularly -- may we please, Registrar, bring up this document on the screen. This is a -- if I'm correct, this is an order issued by Joska Moric in 18th of August, 1995. And my question is, regarding paragraph 2, there was said that: "After today, every case of torching houses, looting should be subject of site investigation." Did you comply this -- with this order?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that we did. I see no reason why we shouldn't have pursued a case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... look at police log-books and compare these documents with other evidence what we gather, what we heard in the -- in the court hearings, we can draw a little bit different conclusion, that, in fact, not all such looting incidents would be subject of on-site investigation. It was also confirmed by Ivo Kardum that criminal police actually did not take any activity regarding these incidents because of lack of people. How could you explain this situation really? What was your other coordinator functions to comply come -- this order, and what steps you directly did?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember these problems but these are the duties of the crime police which were not within my competence. But in principle as far as I know, the basic police reacted to every report, and attended the scene and the crime police was also duly informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, if I have correct information, based on Ivo Kardum testimony, he -- he informed Chamber that, in fact, he did not receive any information about crimes, like loot -- like burning and looting from your -- from Knin, and how it was possible that international observers observe many such accidents but police did not observe anyone?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot challenge Mr. Kardum's claims. What I do know is that we acted duly in response to all reports and, as far as I know, there was no reason whatsoever to gloss over such incidents or not to process them. I allow for the possibility that there were some instances because we were unable to physically cover them all that were left out, but whenever the police station received any such reports or information, or whenever an individual police officer observed any such incident, that had -- action had to be duly taken on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, I would like to read a small portion from the statement that was shown to you and which is not in evidence; that is, the Official Note which was put to you, that is the Official Note compiled on the 13th of October, 2001. It relates to the Grubori situation, and it describes what you reportedly have said as follows: "He," and that's you, "he designated police patrols that were to go to the incident scene. Shortly afterwards, he was telephoned by the assistant minister Joska Moric from the MUP headquarters in Zagreb who told him that it was not necessary to send police patrols to the incident scene because special police members would go there instead." It continues: "He remembers that he remarked that police officers would need to be sent to the incident scene in any case in order to determine the veracity of the UN members' report." A little bit further on, you are reported to have stated that after you had received the instruction to follow orders and not send police officers to the incident scene: "He followed the order and the police patrols did not go to the scene, but whether members of the special police went to the scene or not, he does not know." Could you tell me whether this reflects what you stated, and, if not, explain to what extent it does not.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was just a personal interpretation on the part of someone who was close by when all this was happening. Mr. Moric just told me in a couple of words that I should not concern myself with the duties of the crime police but that I should concern myself with the job assigned to me and that I should leave that to others, i.e., the crime police. I think that he probably meant the crime police, that is. I saw that there was no need for us to continue to pursue that task, and we applied ourselves to other duties that were waiting for us that day. We ceased all activities of the fundamental, the uniformed police. That is, in respect of Grubori.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I'd like you to tell us, in what respect not what happened but what is not correct in what you said. One of the things you mentioned is you said it's just the interpretation of someone, and someone might have meant crime police instead of -- because you referred to the special police being sent there; at least that is how it is reported. Is it -- do you say that at that time you told -- or you stated that the crime police would be sent there instead of, as it's written down here, that the special police would be sent there?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is certain that now, after 13 years have passed, I cannot remember every single word that I said. I remember the incident, and, on the whole, what was going on. I agreed the procedure with Mr. Ivica Cetina, and I was sure that that procedure would be followed. It was only Mr. Moric's call that actually put a stop to the activity of the fundamental police, but I did believe that the crime police would continue that work and undertake every necessary step.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In this statement it is written down what you would have said, and that is that in this telephone conversation, Mr. Moric told you that it was not necessary to send the police because special police members would go there instead. Is that what Mr. Moric told you and what you told the person that interviewed you on the 13th of October, 2001?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That interview, too, in 2001, also took place after many years had elapsed. I cannot remember the interview verbatim, and I cannot remember the talk with Mr. Moric in detail. But I do not remember that detail; namely, that he mentioned the special police. To the best of my recollection, he said that they knew where the bodies were and that that would be processed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you tell, during your interview, that you did not know whether members of the special police went to the scene or not?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are talking about my interview with the ICTY investigators or my talk with Mr. Moric?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm now talking about the interview of which an Official Note was compiled on the 13th of October, 2001, and compiled by a police official, Ivica Vesel. That was the document that was briefly shown to you during your examination.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In respect of that Official Note, I have already stated that I maintain that it was compiled in an unprofessional manner. Because my conversation with the gentleman was a very brief one, and he didn't take down anything that was being said on that occasion. Actually, I had the impression that this was just a pro forma interview to satisfy some formal requirements, by way of preparations for my talk with the UN investigators. I claim that actually the note was compiled by this gentleman on the basis of what he remembered and on the basis of what he knew about the entire situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And he would have known, then, that did you not know whether the special police went there? Is that what you are telling? Because that is what the document tells us. He's talking about you: "But whether members of the special police went to the scene or not, he does not know," and he is referring to you. Is that -- how could that person, Mr. Vesel, know whether you knew or did not know whether the special police went to the scene?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are all assumptions on the part of that gentleman. It is evident from that note that I was informed -- I had been informed of that report a day before. Actually, until I had seen the documents in the log of events, I was convinced that that report had come on the second day in the morning. So just this one detail shows me that it was -- that this note was written by Mr. Vesel, drawing on some other sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. "Other sources" would have told him what you did remember or did not remember?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had either talked to colleagues in the crime police, who are more familiar with the incident, because much was already being said about it; or else he had found some documents that relate to the incident. I didn't say everything that he wrote down there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, do you have any knowledge on -- on what other sources? Do you know names of persons that were interviewed by Mr. Vesel that would have given the information you say he had drawn from other sources, rather than from you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vesel works for the crime police at the headquarters of the Ministry of the Interior. His colleagues who work with him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I put a very precise question to you. Could you give me the names of persons that were interviewed and would have provided to Mr. Vesel the information about what you knew and what you did not know?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know the names of those persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any concrete information that, in relation to what he did write down here, that he interviewed other persons at all?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information, but it is obvious that there is a lot of information about what was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you said it's clear what -- for what purpose this note was prepared, because I think you said it was in order to prepare you for the ICTY interview. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, actually, I'm not clear on why that note was compiled and the interview was actually conducted at my request, in order for me to prepare myself for the interview with the investigators. Such an interview, in my opinion, was not -- such a kind of interview was not actually conducted, in my view, but just a formal interview in order to satisfy this request of mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you explain what the purpose is of being interviewed by a Croatian MUP officer in order to prepare for your ICTY -- Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'm just looking at the dates that appear on the ICTY statement and the dates that appear on this statement and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm looking at it as well. Mr. Buhin, when -- let me just find the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, is it possible -- I'm sorry. Is it possible for to us have access to that? Since it is not an exhibit, it's not in evidence, we don't have a way to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is uploaded. It has a 65 ter number so --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. That would be fine --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- under the circumstances -- of course, if you need a hard copy. I asked for a printout because the Judges have no access to documents that have never reached the status of MFI and I think I announced already that we would -- might consider what to do with that document at any later stage when it was put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I think you did, Your Honour. Just for reference, if you have the 65 ter handy, it would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't have it. I just asked it to be printed off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can inform Mr. Registrar that it is 65 ter 2786.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Buhin, you said you asked for an interview to be held in order for you to prepare for your ICTY interview.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were not yet interviewed by ICTY investigators prior to the interview you had with the -- Mr. Vesel?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The interview with Mr. Vesel was a few days prior to my interview with officials of the Tribunal at The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the -- the Official Note says that although the Official Note was compiled on the 13th of October, 2001, that the interview was conducted on the 9th of October, 2001; whereas, your witness statement gives as dates of interviews, the ones in 2001, 15th and 16th of September.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That confirms yet once again what I have stated; namely, that that note was written subsequently when someone asked for it. And Mr. Vesel could not even remember, nor did he try to recall the date on which we talked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you speak with him then? You said he could not remember nor did he try to recall the date on which you talked. How do you know?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know because he put the wrong dates on his note. We started talking and when I realized that he was unable to help me prepare myself for my interview with the ICTY officials, we actually did not talk for a long time. The conversation was discontinued, and the -- that official did -- was not taking any notes during that interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But how did you know that he gave the wrong dates for the interview? Do you have any clear recollection on what other date than this interview was held with you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say, but I'm quite certain that it was before my interview with the ICTY officials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if I understand your testimony well, what you're telling us is that Mr. Vesel interviewed you; that he just wrote down what others had told him rather than what you told him, because the interview was too short for that; that it was just for formal reasons that this interview was held, although you asked for it, in order to be prepared for an interview which, if we would believe the dates to be correct, was held already some weeks before that. Is that your testimony, Mr. Buhin?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To the extent I was able to follow you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there was any matter unclear, please tell me. Then I'll -- because it is an answer with some reservation in it. Is there any point which you had difficulties in following me?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to follow what you're saying, and you've said it the way it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you say that I actually -- actually -- accurately summarized the portions of your evidence I referred to?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you aware of other persons that were interviewed for the -- by the Office of the Prosecutor, to be interviewed by Croatian police authorities prior to or after the time statements were taken from potential witnesses?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of several colleagues from the police only, as having had interviews with representatives of the ICTY. Now, I am not aware of them having had interviews with representatives of the Croatian police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were the only one you are aware of that had such an interview with the Croatian police?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, I was the first one to be invited to the interview with ICTY officials. I was fearful of the interview. I didn't know which course it would take, what I should say, and I asked for the assistance of the Croatian authorities, of the police in that matter. That's why I was probably the only one, because I was the first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said you didn't know what course it would take and what you should say. Now, you are a trained police officer and you're even recorded in the Official Note as a -- by profession a lawyer, specializing in criminal law, and you -- your testimony now is that you didn't know what to do during an interview. May I suggest to that you the only thing one could reasonably do is to tell the truth to questions that are put to you, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. However, I was the first one and I was apprehensive of how the interview would unfold, whether I would be apprehended or whether my words would be put to someone else. That's why I wanted a representative from the police or from other agencies of the Croatian government to be present there with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I can imagine that you seek guidance as what will happen, but what we find in the Official Note is, apparently, an interview on the substance of the matters, not on the issues you just raised.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was for that reason that I said that the interview with the colleague from the crime police was very short. Because I realized that he was not able to provide me the assistance I sought, our conversation didn't take long, and we parted ways.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, not interview, conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then he started writing a three-page document in which he refers to what you apparently would have told him about, among other matters, the Grubori incident. He just invented all of that, or got it from other sources, as you said?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he got that information from other sources. He didn't get all that information from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I move subjects. You said that you never personally observed stolen goods being transported by HV vehicles. You also explained that it was reported to you what had been seen at the check-points, and you explained to us that it was very difficult to find out whether these were goods which could be legitimately used by the Croatian forces or that these would be stolen goods. Now, you explained to us - I think it was yesterday - what was reported to you as being on these vehicles, which were doors, windows, all kind of household supplies, and you added to that whatever you can load on a truck. That apparently was reported to you. You said it was just rumours about stolen goods being transported. Could you explain to me why you considered that just to be rumours, in view of what was reported to you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the records from check-points, they were many cases of confiscation of various items that, according to the information we had, had been stolen, and there were attempts at taking them out of the area. At the same time, the situation prevailed that made us believe that whatever went through check-points and was within Croatian army vehicles did not necessarily to be for the needs for the Croatian army. This was a belief that prevailed at that time, and as I said today, that cannot be substantiated in any way. The needs of the army were quite extensive and a very broad term, and there is no fundamental evidence in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me re-read your answer. Now, what cannot be substantiated in any way? You say that the view that all those goods were not necessarily for the army, is that a belief, you say, that could not be substantiated?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the -- you say, the windows and the doors and these kind of materials and whatever you could load on a truck, there was no -- you would still consider it a reasonable explanation that the Croatian army was having new doors and windows in its premises. Is that how I have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is not a proper understanding. I said that whatever could be stripped down and taken away was taken away, among other things, doors and windows. I didn't say that they were transported on the military vehicles. I said that there were attempts at transporting these items out of the area that was under our control. Most often such items were found on civilian individuals who wanted to use the material to repair the damage and reconstruct their own homes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When I asked you questions about this yesterday, it was clearly in the context of military vehicles. I asked you about what you could see at a distance of 20 or 30 metres where the military check-point was. You then said that it was -- you couldn't know because it was in -- what did you say about the cars not visible. And then when I later put some questions to you still in the same context, you described what was observed as being on the trucks and what was reported to you, although you had not seen it yourself. But you would say doors, windows, that was all on civilian vehicles, and household appliances, everything you could load onto a truck. That is purely limited to civilian vehicles.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. We were able to control them and see what they transported. We could -- we cannot comment on the ones we weren't able to see what they carried.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll not repeat questions I earlier asked you in this respect. One final matter. You explained to us that the military police refused to be -- to have joint check-points, and you said that was also one of the things that triggered the order to set up joint check-points and to engage in joint patrols. That was -- I think it was the same order of the 19th of August issued by Mr. Moric. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That followed after the order issued and after the meeting by Mr. Moric and Mr. Lausic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, these check-points that were not joint check-points, you told us that sometimes they would have a check-point at a distance of 20 metres. Was that before the 19th of August?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, in response to the efforts to have joint check-points, it was put to you in one of the questions that the military police did not have sufficient people for joint check-points. You remember, not sufficient manpower to have all joint check-points. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember their particular problem but it had to do the entire area of the Knin-Kotar, the Knin district. We engaged in this effort on all the roads in that area, in these joint patrols, though some minor roads may have been covered by the civilian police only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So finally, your check-points were joint check-points?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After the 19th of August, and after the information from Messrs. Moric and Lausic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So therefore the answer, we don't have sufficient people to man joint check-points ...

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where up until the 19th of August there had existed separate check-points of the civilian and military police forces, these check-points merged and separate check-points ceased to exist. Where the military police was unable to provide personnel to man those, the civilian police stepped in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And to that extent, they were not joint anymore. Because I have to -- I try to understand if the military police has no -- let me put it the following way. You said where the check-points were already -- although at a short distance, civilian, military, there they merged, and other check-points, where there was not a military check-point nearby, there it was because of lack of manpower, you say, there it was just civilian check-points. It was manned by the civilian police only?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give me an impression what percentage was joint check-points after this change of attitude or change of policy. What was -- how -- what was the percentage of your check-points that were joint check-points with the military police after the 19th of August? Was it half; was it 25 percent; was it 80 per cent? I'm not asking for a precise figure but just to get an impression.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you precise figures because the area involved is a large one, and I don't remember that anymore. To the extent I remember, between 60 and 70 per cent of the check-points were joint check-points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, I'd like to take you back to the questions that Mr. Margetts asked you, and with respect to keeping track of people that were in the area, there may be the suggestion later that you were able to monitor all of these civilians that had come back in the area. If you recall, I showed you a video of 500 people coming on a train, that there were allegedly 2.000 to 3.000 people in Knin on the 15th of August. Was the police keeping track of all civilians that had returned to the area?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was physically impossible. Only at the time the first civilians were coming in, passes were issued. As larger numbers of people started flooding in, the procedure of issuing passes was abandoned, simply because it was not feasible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So although you were concerned about terrorists, did that mean that, as a result of that concern, you knew everything that was happening in the area concerning civilians?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were concerned about terrorists. We were concerned about perpetrators of criminal offences. However, it was only a selective control and checks of suspicious individuals, individuals suspected of having committed something wrong. Checks were made but they were far insufficient, given the size of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Obviously we haven't confirmed the specific date where we could say there were a large number of civilians coming in. You've talked about the freedom train; I've showed you other reports. But whenever that date is, whenever that began to happen, is it safe to say that the liberated territory essentially was a free territory just as the same as, for example, the territory on the coast?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When passes were abolished, and that was before the first train service from Zagreb to Split became operational via Knin -- I'm sorry, I seem to have got lost. Can you please repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me phrase it a different way. When did the liberated territory begin to get treated, in terms of freedom of movement for civilians, just like any other part of Croatia? For example, the coastal Croatia.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the day the passes were abolished.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Judge Gwaunza asked you a question about HV troops returning from Bosnia and then looting and burning. Were these the soldiers that you were referring to in your testimony earlier this week, the demobilized soldiers?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as it was subsequently confirmed, among the perpetrators of crimes, there were demobilized soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you refer to soldiers that had come back from Bosnia and committed crimes. Is your testimony that these people returned from Bosnia, were demobilized, and then committed crime?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that this needs to -- for any useful evidence to be provided, it would be helpful if this was taken in stages. I'm not entirely sure what the basis for this witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Until now, Mr. Margetts used such general terms that it hardly could have done any major harm. You may continue, and whether or not you will follow the advise of Mr. Margetts is up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me repeat my question, sir. Is it your testimony that these people returned from Bosnia, were demobilized, and then committed crime, as demobilized soldiers?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is based on the knowledge of my colleagues from the ministry who were involved in crime investigation activities. There were such cases where persons, having been demobilized, went back to their localities which had been devastated. They engaged in unlawful activities, such as taking items from a home and then using them as material for their own houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In your answer you say "having been demobilized." Again, let me make sure that is clear. You're saying having been demobilized after returning from Bosnia? Is that what you heard?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm that in relation to them having returned from Bosnia. Individuals who were members of armed units were demobilized and went home. Now, which front lines they had originally come from is something that I cannot make any definite statement about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, in your statement when you make reference to soldiers returning from Bosnia, where did you get the information that they were coming back from Bosnia from?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that. I probably remembered at that time General Cermak promising that, at some of the meetings, that the army would be redirected from the Knin front lines elsewhere, probably some of the troops went to Bosnia as well, and it must have been in that context that I mentioned Bosnia. I don't have any other knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So you have no specific knowledge of any troops that came back from Bosnia and committed crime. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I can't pinpoint the location.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: With respect to this issue of doors and windows on trucks, you've clarified what your testimony was yesterday. However, let me just ask you, the Trial Chamber has heard a lot of evidence about smashed windows that occurred during Operation Storm, other damage to buildings that took place as a result of the operations. How did new windows, new doors, new building materials, et cetera, are you aware of whether the Croatian army also participated in transporting materials that were used to reconstruct items that were damaged during military operations? Are you aware that the Croatian army also participated in the delivery of those types of items?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At no point in time did we discuss new doors and windows. There were cases where persons, having returned to their homes that had been damaged, would go to other homes, other properties, stripping them of doors and windows in order for them to use them on their own homes. I don't have any knowledge about materials being transported by the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Buhin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mikulicic, I have one short follow-up question on Mr. Misetic's questions. Perhaps you might need this one as well. Mr. Buhin, you talked about demobilized soldiers returning to the place where they came from. Now, once they were demobilized, once they had returned to their villages, would they, upon their return, would they fall within the jurisdiction of the civilian police, the normal -- ordinary police, or would they still be under the jurisdiction of the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot say with precision, but I do believe that a large part who had been demobilized were returned to the normal civilian walks of life and were treated as civilians. It should be underlined that, at that time, the HV uniform was extremely popular and that people continued wearing it even after demobilization and that many such persons walked around the town of Zagreb, whereas there was no need for that at all. It simply was the vogue and the image that was popular.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We've seen some statistics on abuse of uniforms and civilians and military. I have no further questions. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'll try be to be very short, Your Honour. Can I have on the screen, please, D527.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Buhin, just a couple of questions that I'm prompted to ask by your answers to the question of the His Honour, the Presiding Judge. We shall now see on our screens a document that we have already seen and that is the decree on the internal organisation and manner of work of the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Croatia. Can we see Article 27 of this document, the identification number is 3D00-1514. What we shall see right now, Mr. Buhin, is the Article which regulates the structure of the special police sector within the framework of the Ministry of the Interior. Article 27 states that the sector of the special police shall, in fact, have eight components: An internal control department; and an anti-terrorist combat detail; a special anti-terrorist detail; an air force unit. The third one is Lucko air force unit; five, psychological propaganda department; six, special police logistics department; a department for training and utilisation of police dogs and horses; and a training centre. As you can see, Mr. Buhin, nowhere within the structure of the special police do we see any crime unit. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you, Mr. Buhin, during your long years of service as a police officer, ever see members of the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry will Defence counsel please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, the interpreters have not -- have not followed your question. Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the sake of interpretation, Mr. Buhin, and I'm, of course, rushing because we are behind schedule. I asked you: Did you ever see or hear that members of the special police ever conducted the crime processing of any case?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have never seen nor heard of anything -- never seen anything like that nor heard of anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So when Mr. Vesel, in his note, wrote that he had allegedly talked with you or, rather, that you had said that a special police unit would be sent to the scene of the event to investigate, that is something that is actually not at all logical in view of your police work experience and knowledge?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So can you confirm that you actually never said anything of the kind?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Have you at all, Mr. Buhin, in this brief conversation that you asked -- that you requested yourself with Mr. Vesel, did you at all discuss the incident in the village of Grubori?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably did mention that we would also be talking about that too, but I did not discuss it in detail with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Margetts. I'm looking at the clock and I have not yet even asked the interpreters and the others, which I should have done, whether we could continue for a couple of minutes. Unless there is something very urgent that can you deal with in one minute, I would ask you to consider whether there's an absolute need to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, there's not an absolute need, no. I -- I could deal with it probably in a couple of minutes, though, if we had a couple of minutes. Maybe not one, but two or three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two or three. I'm looking at the booth. If I keep a close eye on the clock and limit Mr. Margetts to two and a half minutes, would you -- two and a half. And I don't receive an answer. Sometimes if something is not denied, I assume it is granted. Two and a half minutes and I will be very strict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and thank you interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Buhin, in the course of answering His Honour's questions, His Honour Judge Orie's questions, you made a distinction between civilian vehicles and military vehicles. The question was: But you would say doors, windows, that was all on civilian vehicles, and household appliances, everything you could load on to a truck. That is purely limited to civilian vehicles. Your answer was: Precisely so. We were able to control them and see what they transported. We could -- we cannot comment on the ones we weren't able to see what they carry. When you said "the ones," were you referring to military vehicles?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN BUHIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And what was your understanding, who could control the movement of military vehicles?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that triggered by my questions? And I think -- I refrained from further questions because if you would careful look at the transcript of the evidence given earlier on what you could see, what you couldn't see, what were trucks which were open, trucks which were not open, I thought that I was sufficiently informed. I did not raise an issue of who, then, were the competent authorities to deal with the matter. That certain has not been triggered by my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Buhin, this then concludes your testimony in this Court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for answering the many, many questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench. And I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we adjourn, and we resume tomorrow, the 9th of October, quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon, Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 9th day of October, 2008, at 2.15 p.m. 25
